title: A Click Then a Murmur / Common, Usually Benign, But Know Who Needs Follow-up

blocks.text: A Click Then a Murmur / Common, Usually Benign, But Know Who Needs Follow-up

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-10 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: British Society of Echocardiography, Clinical indications and triage of echocardiography: heart valve disease (July 2024); ESC Guidelines on sports cardiology and exercise in patients with cardiovascular disease (2020); NICE CG64 Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis (published 17 March 2008; last updated 8 July 2016) · Related AMaC: AMaC mitral regurgitation with AF station; this one tests prolapse with a mild leak
The patient is a woman of 28 who works as a physiotherapist. She has occasional palpitations and an abnormal sound heard at a routine check. Please examine her cardiovascular system.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex is mitral valve prolapse. It is common and usually benign; the marks come from knowing which patients need closer follow-up.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates hear a murmur and call it mitral regurgitation or aortic stenosis, then either alarm her or discharge her. Pass: click then late murmur, standing makes it more obvious, and follow-up by risk. Fail: wrong valve, or no follow-up plan.

rows: Think
Say
Do
She is well. Look carefully: the click is the diagnosis, and her build may point to a connective tissue cause.
"May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit her at 45 degrees; hands, face, build, pulse, JVP; chest wall.
Time the click against the apex beat, then listen after she stands.
"I'm going to listen over the heart lying down, then standing, and ask you to breathe out."
Apex; thrill; four areas; axilla; click timing; stand and re-listen; carotids; lung bases; ankles; cover her.
Name the lesion, grade the leak by what you find, and say who needs follow-up.
"She has mitral valve prolapse with a mild leak. I'd confirm it with echocardiography and arrange follow-up by risk."
Present in order; diagnosis; complications; echo; follow-up interval; red flags; thank her.

Systematic technique
Disorganised; omits the pulse, apex or axilla, or does not re-listen standing.
Hands, pulse, JVP, apex, four auscultation areas, axilla, then re-listens standing, then carotids and lung bases.
Also leans her forward in held expiration and checks the build and arm span.
R3
B
Identifying signs
Reports a diastolic murmur, a thrill or heart failure that is not present.
Finds a mid-systolic click and a late systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, more obvious standing.
Also states occasional ectopic beats, no thrill or failure, and no Marfan features.
R4
D
Differential diagnosis
Calls it aortic stenosis or a ventricular septal defect.
Mitral valve prolapse with a mild leak.
Also separates it from rheumatic regurgitation and a secondary cause, such as connective tissue disease.
R5
E
Investigations and follow-up
Discharges with no echo, or orders an echo every year for everyone.
Asks for echocardiography, and says asymptomatic people with a mild leak are seen every 3 to 5 years.
Also asks for ECG and Holter if she has palpitations, and gives the factors that shorten the interval.
R6
E
Risks and advice
Tells her to stop all exercise, or that nothing can go wrong.
Names regurgitation, arrhythmia, stroke and rarely sudden death, and says normal exercise is fine once echo and rhythm assessment show no high-risk features.
Also says unexplained fainting or a family history of sudden death needs specialist review before competitive sport.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: slim, comfortable at rest; respiratory rate 14; pulse 74, regular apart from occasional ectopic beats; blood pressure 112/68; SpO2 99% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Hands: normal; arm span equal to height. Palate normal. JVP not raised. Apex beat in the fifth space, mid-clavicular line, not displaced; no thrill. Mid-systolic click at the apex, followed by a late systolic murmur radiating to the axilla; the click comes earlier and the murmur is longer and louder standing. Second sound normal. Lungs clear. No oedema.

Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B, R3) Mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur at the apex, more obvious standing; occasional ectopics; no thrill or failure. 2. Diagnosis? (D, R4) Mitral valve prolapse with a mild leak. 3. Complications? (E, R6) Regurgitation, arrhythmia, stroke, rarely sudden death. 4. Investigation and follow-up? (E, R5) Echocardiography; ECG and Holter for palpitations; echo every 3 to 5 years if asymptomatic with a mild leak (BSE 2024). 5. Who needs closer follow-up? (E, R5) Moderate or severe regurgitation, symptoms, LV dilatation, LVEF below 60%, raised pulmonary pressure, new atrial fibrillation.

Curveballs: She mentions a faint on exercise last month: urgent cardiology review, echo, ECG and rhythm monitoring, and no competitive sport until assessed. Can she exercise? Yes, if the echo and rhythm assessment show no high-risk features; a well person with mild regurgitation need not restrict activity. Does she need antibiotics before dental work? No; NICE CG64 advises against routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures.

CANDIDATE: Sit back. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Listens at the apex lying flat only.) [R2 Fail] There's an early diastolic murmur. [R3 Fail] It's aortic stenosis. [R4 Fail]

CANDIDATE: No echo needed; discharge. [R5 Fail] Stop all exercise. [R6 Fail]
Examiner note: No consent, listening only lying flat, a murmur invented, the wrong valve named, no echo or follow-up, and exercise banned without reason.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, pulse, JVP, apex, four areas, axilla; listens again standing; carotids; bases.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: There is a mid-systolic click and a late systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, more obvious standing. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Mitral valve prolapse with a mild leak. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Investigation and follow-up?
CANDIDATE: Echocardiography. If asymptomatic with a mild leak, review every 3 to 5 years. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Risks?
CANDIDATE: Regurgitation, arrhythmia, stroke and rarely sudden death; she can exercise normally once the echo and rhythm assessment show no high-risk features. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not separate it from other lesions or name the features that shorten the follow-up interval.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) May I examine your heart? Would you like a chaperone? I'll keep you covered and check you are steady when standing. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, arm span, pulse, JVP, apex, four areas, axilla; leans her forward in held expiration; re-listens standing.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur radiating to the axilla, more obvious standing; occasional ectopics; no thrill, failure or Marfan features. [R3 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Mitral valve prolapse with a mild leak, not rheumatic regurgitation; connective tissue disease can cause a secondary form. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Investigation and follow-up?
CANDIDATE: Echo, and ECG and Holter for her palpitations. Every 3 to 5 years if asymptomatic with a mild leak; sooner for moderate or severe leak, fainting or a worse echo. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Risks?

CANDIDATE: Fainting or a family history of sudden death needs specialist review before competitive sport; otherwise normal exercise once the echo, rhythm monitoring and family history are reviewed. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands, thanks her.) [R1 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone, arm span, held-expiration listening, the secondary cause, rhythm monitoring, shorter follow-up factors and sport advice.
R2: Listening only lying flat. The click and murmur are more obvious standing, so the diagnostic sign may be missed.
R4: Naming aortic stenosis. The click and a late systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla point to the mitral valve.
R5: No echo or follow-up plan. The leak is never graded, and she cannot be told when to return.

R6: Banning exercise. Patients without high-risk features can exercise normally, and the advice turns a benign finding into a disability. Equally, saying all is well without echo and rhythm assessment misses those at risk.
"May I stand her up and listen again?"
"The click is at the apex with a late murmur, so I'd say mitral valve prolapse."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"

Mitral valve prolapse: a mid- or late-systolic click and a late-systolic or pansystolic murmur, more obvious on standing. Complications include regurgitation, arrhythmia, stroke, atrial fibrillation and rarely sudden death.

Asymptomatic with a mild leak: echo surveillance every 3 to 5 years, because a prolapsing valve is anatomically abnormal (BSE 2024). Closer follow-up and cardiology review for moderate or severe regurgitation, symptoms, LV dilatation, LVEF below 60%, raised pulmonary pressure or new atrial fibrillation (BSE 2024).

Red flags needing specialist review before competitive sport: unexplained fainting and a family history of sudden death. The ESC sports cardiology guidelines 2020 advise an exercise test and 24-hour ECG for everyone with prolapse, name myocardial scarring, mitral annular disjunction, inferior T-wave inversion and ventricular arrhythmia arising from the left ventricle as high-risk markers, and allow all sport in asymptomatic people with mild or moderate regurgitation who have none of them. Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work is not routinely recommended (NICE CG64).
THINK: Click then late murmur: prolapse; follow-up by risk.
SAY: "Mitral valve prolapse with a mild leak."
DO: Re-listen standing; check the axilla.
NUMBERS: Mild leak: echo every 3 to 5 years (BSE, July 2024).
TRAP: Wrong valve; banning exercise.
FINISH: Echo, Holter if palpitations; fainting needs review.

Eur Heart J 2021;42:17-96. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaa605 Supports: evaluation (exercise test, 24-hour ECG) and sport advice for people with mitral valve prolapse; high-risk markers.
